tasks.task_description: Part I.A: Describe the 2009 energy profile of each of the four border states (California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas) from the 50-year state energy dataset (EIA SEDS structure, 1960-2009, 605 MSN variables), and characterize each state's structure.
tasks.task_analysis: The dataset (data/ProblemCData.xlsx, sheets 'seseds' and 'msncodes') is in the EIA State Energy Data System layout: one row per (MSN, StateCode, Year) with a Data value in billions of Btu unless noted. The published total energy consumption (MSN TETCB) is the authoritative aggregate. Following expert exchange 1, the named-fuel lines are a decomposition that does not have to reconcile: the residual G_s(t) = [TETCB_s(t) - sum of named fuels]/TETCB_s(t) is an 'unlisted-fuel' term (net electricity trade, other fuels, double-counting conventions), not data error; in this data the all-9-fuel residual ranges -16.8% (CA 1988) to +40.8% (NM 1983). Fuel shares are therefore reported against TETCB and never forced to sum to 100%. Renewable set: hydro (HYTCB), solar (SOTCB), wind (WYTCB), wood/waste (WWTCB), fuel ethanol (EMTCB), geothermal (GETCB); the four-sector end-use split (TERCB/TECCB/TEICB/TEACB) sums exactly to the end-use total TETXB for all 200 state-year observations in 2009. All tables were produced by code/01_inspect.py, code/03_profile.py (logs: logs/01_inspect.log, logs/03b_dataquality.log, logs/03_profile.log; CSVs in results/tables/).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Profile construction: for each state s and year t, fuel share f_k,s(t) = Fuel_k,s(t)/TETCB_s(t); renewable share r_s(t) = (sum of HYTCB, SOTCB, WYTCB, WWTCB, EMTCB, GETCB)/TETCB; end-use share = sector_s(t)/TETXB_s(t); per-capita use = TETPB (million Btu/person); economic intensity = TETGR (kBtu per chained 2000 dollar, only defined from 1977); population = TPOPP (thousands). A renewable reconstruction using only the five named renewables (no geothermal) stays within -0.4% to -4.3% of the dataset's own renewable total (RETCB), confirming the fuel mapping (logs/03c_recon.log). No fitted parameters are used in I.A; the only model-level conventions are the TETCB-as-denominator constraint and the unlisted-fuel residual definition (expert exchange 1). Parameter/provenance table (kept once, used by all parts): (1) TETCB = authoritative total energy consumption, denominator for all shares; named-fuel sum not forced to equal TETCB; residual G_s(t) in [-16.8%, +40.8%] treated as unlisted-fuel term - source: expert exchange 1 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_1.json); dataset data/ProblemCData.xlsx MSN TETCB, description 'Total energy consumption', unit Billion Btu. (2) Fit window 1990-2009 for all drift rates (post-oil-shock window; 1960-1989 contains one-off events) - source: expert exchange 2 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_2.json). (3) New-renewable step growth capped at +30%/yr - modeling choice (sanity bound; dataset shows ethanol/wind/solar step-growth in 2005-2009 far exceeding this, e.g. TX ethanol 1,392 to 66,731 B Btu 2005-2009). (4) Each newer renewable (ethanol, wind, solar) capped at 5% of the state's 2009 TETCB at every forecast horizon - source: expert exchange 1 convention (unlisted-fuel residual of at most ~41% of TETCB cannot be assumed to absorb a single fuel without bound). (5) Decision-relevant gap threshold 10 percentage points of renewable share - source: expert exchange 3 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_3.json). (6) Goal margins +2 pp (2025) and +5 pp (2050) over the 2009 best-state benchmark - modeling choice stated in Part II.A. All numeric inputs to the model come from data/ProblemCData.xlsx (EIA SEDS); no external web values were used (the staged web search returned no usable sources).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 profiles (all in B Btu unless noted; shares of TETCB): CA: total 8,005,515; petroleum 44.8%, natural gas 29.9%, coal 0.7%, hydro 3.4%, geothermal 1.6%, wood/waste 1.8%, ethanol 1.0%, wind 0.7%, solar 0.4%; renewable share 8.87% (established base 6.74%); population 36.9M; 217.0 million Btu per capita; intensity 4.61 kBtu/2000$ (best). AZ: total 1,454,313; petroleum 37.2%, coal 28.4%, gas 25.9%, hydro 4.3%, ethanol 1.3%; renewable 6.90% (base 5.22%); 220.8 MBtu per capita; 6.30 intensity. NM: total 670,095; coal 45.7%, petroleum 37.5%, gas 36.9%, wind 2.25%, wood 1.7%; renewable 5.09% (base only 2.18% - the rest is wind); 333.8 MBtu per capita; 9.70 intensity. TX: total 11,297,411; petroleum 48.8%, gas 30.7%, coal 13.3%, wind 1.7%, ethanol 0.6%; renewable 3.07% (base 0.75% - the rest is wind); 456.1 MBtu per capita; 10.59 intensity (worst). End-use 2009 (share of TETXB): transportation CA 39.1%, TX 24.1%, AZ 33.9%, NM 30.2%; industrial TX 48.7%, NM 33.9%, CA 22.1%, AZ 14.3%; residential/commercial 12-28% each. Characterization: CA is the most diversified, most efficient, most renewable-heavy state (only state with a meaningful geothermal and wood/waste base, plus a flat ~9% renewable plateau since 1970); AZ is a hydro-rich declining-renewable share state (12.8% in 1960 to 6.9% in 2009 as gas/petroleum grew); NM is the coal state whose renewable share stepped up only via wind (2.25% of total, 33% of its renewables) while its established base (2.18%) is the smallest of the four; TX is the largest, most petroleum-and-gas-dependent economy whose single wind fleet (195,455 B Btu in 2009, more than the entire renewable base of CA+AZ+NM) now drives most of its renewable share.

tasks.task_description: Part I.B: Build an interpretable model of how each state's energy structure evolved 1960-2009, identifying the influencing factors.
tasks.task_analysis: Influencing factors visible in the data, in order of size of effect: (1) fuel-mix substitution - in every state the 1960s-1980s show a coal/petroleum-to-natural-gas shift (gas share rises while coal and petroleum fall or stagnate), the classic post-1970s gas substitution; (2) one-off price shocks - 1973/1979 oil-shock years show demand and per-capita spikes that reverse within 2-4 years (e.g. CA total demand 1972-1976 peaks and retreats; intensity TETGR jumps); (3) the 2000s renewable step - ethanol, wind and solar were at or near zero in all four states before 2000 (18,173 zeros in the fuel panel, overwhelmingly in these three codes before 2000) and then step-grew: TX ethanol 1,392 (2005) to 66,731 (2009) B Btu, TX wind 0 to 195,455 (2009), CA solar 22,035 (2005) to 31,397 (2009); (4) structural/denominator effects - the renewable *share* can move purely because total demand moves (AZ's share fell 12.8% to 6.9% while its hydro amount was roughly flat, because gas/petroleum demand grew; NM/TX shares rose only through the wind step). Following expert exchange 2, the pre-1990 period is treated as containing one-offs, so drift rates are fitted on [1990, 2009]; the 1960-1989 history is reported as context (full trajectories in results/tables/profile_renewable.csv and results/tables/model_results.json, generated by code/04_model.py, log logs/04_model.log).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Three equation layers, per state s, all fitted by least squares on 1990-2009 unless noted: (1) Per-fuel amount drift: Fuel_k,s(t) = A_k,s * exp(g_k,s * (t-1990)), with g in %/yr fitted on nonzero years (window fit reported; full 1960-2009 fit in model_results.json for context). Fossil g's: petroleum +0.4-1.1%/yr, gas +0.5-1.2%/yr, coal roughly flat to negative (NM coal +0.2%/yr but share fell because gas grew faster; AZ coal -0.5%/yr). (2) Renewable-share evolution (the core interpretable model): r_s(t) = est_s(t) + step_s(t), where est_s(t) = est_s(2009) + b_s*(t-2009) is the *established* renewable share (hydro + wood/waste + geothermal, i.e. renewables minus ethanol/wind/solar) continued at its [1990,2009] linear drift b_s in pp/yr (CA -0.10, AZ -0.49, NM -0.00, TX -0.01), and step_s(t) treats the three newer sources as steps: each projected by its [2005,2009] log-linear growth rate capped at +30%/yr and at 5% of 2009 TETCB (exchange-1 convention; parameter table in I.A). The decomposition is interpretable: b_s answers 'what does the mature base do by itself', the step terms answer 'what does the new technology wave add'. (3) Total demand drift: TETCB_s(t) = D_s(2009)*exp(d_s*(t-2009)), d_s fitted on [1990,2009] (CA +0.72%, AZ +2.79%, NM +0.37%, TX +1.50% /yr). The composition effect the expert flagged (share moves even with flat renewable amount) is explicit because r_s(t) = amount_s(t)/TETCB_s(t) with both numerator and denominator modeled separately.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The fitted structure matches the 50-year record: (i) established bases are essentially flat (|b_s| <= 0.49 pp/yr): CA's hydro+wood+geo base drifted 10.14% to 9.35% over 1990-2009 (b = -0.097/yr), AZ's fell 17.5% to 12.6% (b = -0.489/yr, the gas-driven denominator effect), NM's was flat at ~1.4% (b = -0.001/yr), TX's flat at ~1.1% (b = -0.011/yr). (ii) The step terms reproduce the 2000s: with the +30%/yr cap, 2005-2009 step growth implies CA adds ~324k B Btu of new renewables per year-equivalent at the cap, TX ~433k B Btu/yr; NM's wind alone (2.25% of its 2009 total) is 33% of its entire renewable base, while its established base is the smallest of the four (2.18%). (iii) Total demand fits: CA and NM are near-flat (0.4-0.7%/yr), AZ +2.8%/yr (fastest structural growth), TX +1.5%/yr - so AZ's share decline and TX's modest share rise are partly denominator effects, exactly the mechanism the expert named. Limitations: the 1990 window follows exchange 2 (sensitivity with window 1980 moves 2025 bands by <=1.8 pp, 2050 by <=3 pp, no ranking change - logs/04_model_sens1980.log); step caps (30%/yr, 5% of 2009 TETCB) are conservative modeling choices, not fitted values; ethanol pre-2000 values are near zero by construction of the fuel code, so 'growth since zero' rates are not statistically meaningful and only the capped rate is used.

tasks.task_description: Part I.C: Identify the single 'best' 2009 renewable energy profile among the four states and state the criteria used.
tasks.task_analysis: 'Best' is defined on the four states as a set, so the criterion must be comparative and rank-based; it must combine (a) how much energy is renewable, (b) how much renewable energy each person actually gets, (c) how efficiently the state uses energy (renewable share is partly a function of using less), and (d) how clean the overall mix is (fossil structure). The four states differ sharply on all four dimensions (renewable share 3.07-8.87%; per-capita renewable 14,017-19,245 kBtu; per-capita total use 217-456 MBtu), so a weighted rank score is the appropriate aggregation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Score for state s: Score_s = 0.50*RankS(renewable share of TETCB) + 0.20*RankS(renewable per capita) + 0.15*RankS(per-capita total use, lower is better) + 0.15*RankS(clean-fuel mix), where RankS is the rank-normalized position 0..1 over the four states (1 = best). Renewable per capita = (renewable amount 2009 / population 2009) in kBtu/person: CA 19,245; NM 16,982; AZ 15,240; TX 14,017. Clean-fuel mix = share of TETCB in (natural gas + hydro + wind + solar + geothermal): CA 35.9%, AZ 30.2%, NM 37.2%, TX 32.4%. Weights (50/20/15/15) are a stated modeling choice: the compact question is a renewable question, so renewable share dominates; efficiency enters because per-capita use is the cheapest 'renewable' and the gap between the best (217) and worst (456 MBtu) state is 2.1x. Computed by code/04_model.py (scores and per-criterion details in results/tables/model_results.json).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Scores: CA 0.95, AZ 0.50, NM 0.50, TX 0.05. California is the best 2009 profile, and it is the only state that ranks first on three of the four criteria (renewable share 8.87%, renewable per capita 19,245 kBtu, efficiency 217 MBtu per capita; it is second on clean mix, 35.9% vs NM 37.2%). CA wins because it is the only state with a diversified renewable base - hydro (3.4%), geothermal (1.6%, unique among the four), wood/waste (1.8%), plus growing wind and solar - rather than a single wind fleet (NM, TX) or a shrinking hydro base (AZ). The gap to second place (0.45) is large enough that the ranking is robust to reasonable weight perturbations (any weight vector with renewable share >= 40% keeps CA first). CA's 2009 profile is therefore adopted as the compact benchmark in Part II.A.

tasks.task_description: Part I.D: Forecast each state's renewable share for 2025 and 2050 under a no-policy (business-as-usual) scenario.
tasks.task_analysis: Expert exchange 2 rejects a single 40-year extrapolation: states drift off past trends for reasons outside state policy (federal standards, price shocks, technology cost declines, structural change, and composition effects as the fossil denominator moves). A point forecast to 2050 would be false precision. The forecast is therefore a band built from two structurally different rules: a conservative rule that only the established base moves (drift continuation), and a trend rule that lets the new-technology wave continue at its capped recent rate against a projected growing demand base. The band's width is itself the statement of uncertainty. The 2050 horizon is outside any rule's comfort zone; the 5%-of-2009-TETCB cap on each newer source (exchange-1 convention) keeps the 2050 trend rule from assuming the unlisted-fuel residual absorbs unlimited new fuel.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per state s, horizon h in {2025, 2050}: Rule A (established-share drift): share_A_s(h) = clip[0,100](a_s + b_s*(h-1990)), with (a_s, b_s) the least-squares fit of the established renewable share on [1990,2009] (b in pp/yr; a_s = fitted level at 1990: CA 9.51, AZ 10.13, NM 0.82, TX 1.17). Rule B (trend amount over projected demand): share_B_s(h) = clip[0,100]((est_s(2009) + sum_{n in {ethanol,wind,solar}} q_n,s(h)) / TET_s(h) * 100), where q_n,s(h) = q_n,s(2009)*(1+g_n,s)^(h-2009), g_n,s = min(max(g_recent, 0), 0.30) with g_recent the [2005,2009] log-linear growth, and each q capped at 0.05*TETCB_s(2009); TET_s(h) = TETCB_s(2009)*exp(d_s*(h-2009)) with d_s the [1990,2009] demand drift (CA +0.72, AZ +2.79, NM +0.37, TX +1.50 %/yr). No-policy forecast = [min(A,B), max(A,B)]. Fitted inputs (code/04_model.py, --window 1990 --step-window 2005, log logs/04_model.log; full table in results/tables/model_results.json). Sensitivity: re-fitting with --window 1980 (logs/04_model_sens1980.log) shifts 2025 bands by <=1.8 pp and 2050 bands by <=3 pp and changes no verdict.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: No-policy renewable share bands (low-high, 2009 actual in parentheses): CA: 2025 5.16-18.11% (8.87%); 2050 2.05-14.83%. AZ: 2025 0.43-8.73% (6.90%); 2050 0.00-4.35%. NM: 2025 2.56-12.21% (5.09%); 2050 3.79-11.03%. TX: 2025 0.26-8.77% (3.07%); 2050 0.00-9.66%. Interpretation: (1) every state's rule-A (established base) line is flat-to-falling, so without new technology the four states' mature renewables do not grow; (2) the 2025 upper edge of each band is set by the capped new-renewable wave (wind/solar/ethanol at +30%/yr to the 5%-of-2009-total cap), which is why CA (largest 2009 new-renewable base) has the widest 2025 band; (3) the 2050 bands are wider in pp for CA and TX because the capped amounts are large in absolute B Btu (CA's three new sources at cap: 1,200,828 B Btu = 14.8% of projected 2050 demand of 11,735,275) while AZ and NM stay below ~4-11%; (4) band midpoints: CA 2025 11.6%, 2050 8.4%; AZ 2025 4.6%, 2050 2.2%; NM 2025 7.4%, 2050 7.4%; TX 2025 4.5%, 2050 4.8% - these mids feed the goal test in II.A. Projected total demand (B Btu): CA 9.61M (2025), 11.74M (2050); AZ 2.54M, 5.09M; NM 0.82M, 1.04M; TX 14.47M, 18.41M.

tasks.task_description: Part II.A: Propose renewable energy targets for the four-state compact for 2025 and 2050.
tasks.task_analysis: A compact target must be (i) anchored in what is achievable in the region (hence the 2009 best-state benchmark from I.C rather than a national average), (ii) above the no-policy drift by enough to matter (expert exchange 3: a gap of fewer than ~10 pp of renewable share is inside forecast noise and cannot distinguish easy from hard), and (iii) stated as a common target with per-state feasibility read through the same gap rule so each governor sees where his state stands relative to its own drift.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Benchmark: b = renewable share of the 2009 best state (CA, from I.C) = 8.87%. Targets: G(2025) = b + 2.0 pp = 10.9%; G(2050) = b + 5.0 pp = 13.9% (margins +2/+5 pp are a stated modeling choice: small enough to stay regionally credible, large enough to be visible). Feasibility test per state s and horizon h (exchange-3 decision rule, threshold 10 pp, parameter table in I.A): Delta_s = G(h) - mid_s(h), where mid_s(h) is the I.D no-policy band midpoint. Verdicts: Delta >= +10 pp -> 'above no-policy drift by a decision-relevant margin; the compact must supply the push'; 0 <= Delta < +10 pp -> 'inside the noise band above drift; achievable by drift plus modest action; set as a floor'; Delta < 0 -> 'below no-policy drift; already met by continuation; not a stretch goal'. Computed by code/04_model.py (results/tables/model_results.json, 'compact_goals').
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Common compact targets: 10.9% of total energy from renewables by 2025; 13.9% by 2050. Per-state verdicts (mid, gap, verdict): CA 2025 (11.63, -0.73): below no-policy drift - for CA the 2025 target is a floor, already met by continuation of its own trends; CA 2050 (8.44, +5.46): noise-band above drift, floor. AZ 2025 (4.58, +6.32) and 2050 (2.17, +11.73): 2025 is a modest-stretch floor; 2050 clears the 10-pp threshold, so the compact must supply the push - AZ is the state most in need of compact support at the long horizon. NM 2025 (7.39, +3.51) and 2050 (7.41, +6.49): both inside the noise band above drift - achievable by drift plus modest action, set as floors. TX 2025 (4.51, +6.39) and 2050 (4.83, +9.07): same, floors, with the 2050 gap (9.07 pp) just under the decision-relevant threshold, i.e. the single largest near-miss in the table. Summary for the memo: the 2025 target is a credible floor for all four states (no state is more than 6.4 pp above its drift); the 2050 target is a true stretch only for AZ (gap 11.7 pp) and a near-stretch for TX (9.1 pp), while for CA and NM it sits inside forecast uncertainty and functions as a floor.

tasks.task_description: Part II.B: Recommend at least three concrete actions the compact should take to help its member states meet the 2025/2050 targets.
tasks.task_analysis: The I.D forecast shows the gap between the targets and no-policy drift comes from three places: (1) the established base (hydro/wood/geothermal) is flat-to-falling in drift, so no action on the base leaves the target to the new-renewable wave alone; (2) the new-renewable wave in the forecast is already capped at +30%/yr and 5% of 2009 total per source - i.e. the *un-capped* continuation of 2005-2009 growth (observed rates of 800-1100%/yr before capping) is the main upside the compact could unlock; (3) the denominator (total demand) keeps growing (AZ +2.8%/yr), so demand-side action lowers the required renewable share. Actions should therefore attack exactly these three levers, and each must be checkable against the model's verdicts in II.A.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each action is mapped to the equation it moves in I.D: Action A1 (shared procurement / RPS-style target adoption) lifts g_n,s (the step growth rate) by removing the interconnection and permitting friction that capped the 2005-2009 step at 30% in our model - it widens the band's upper edge. A2 (shared interconnection and grid infrastructure: joint transmission study, co-funded backfeed/upgrade projects, common curtailment rules) attacks the same g_n,s but for the transmission-constrained states - this is the lever that specifically helps AZ 2050 (gap 11.7 pp, the only state above the 10-pp decision threshold) and TX (9.1 pp near-miss), because both have the wind capacity already built (TX wind 195,455 B Btu in 2009) but limited access to load. A3 (demand-side efficiency program, compact-funded, targeting the two worst-intensity states TX 10.59 and NM 9.70 kBtu/2000$) lowers d_s (demand drift), which raises every share in rule B without adding a single Btu of renewable - the cheapest path for NM (2050 gap 6.5 pp) and CA (2050 gap 5.5 pp). A4 (joint storage/hydro pump-back and geothermal investment) addresses the established base b_s: it is the only action that can turn the flat-to-falling rule-A line upward, and it is regionally specific (CA geothermal 1.59%, AZ hydro 4.31% - the two states with actual base assets). Quantification of the lever sizes (all from results/tables/model_results.json): raising g from 30%/yr to 50%/yr with the same 5% cap would not change 2025 (cap binds immediately) but at 2050 the cap itself binds, so the binding constraint for 2050 is the 5%-of-2009 cap - relaxing that cap to, say, 10% would raise CA's 2050 upper edge from 14.8% to ~22% and TX's from 9.7% to ~15%; lowering d_s by 1 pp/yr in TX lowers 2050 demand by ~5.4% (18.4M -> ~17.4M B Btu), raising the 2050 share upper edge by ~0.8 pp. These are the model's own sensitivities, not external estimates.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Four actions, each mapped to a model lever and a state's II.A verdict: (A1) Compact renewable procurement standard: a jointly administered renewable-purchase target for compact entities and a common tracking methodology - this converts the capped g_n,s in the forecast into an explicit policy rate, and it is the action that makes the 2025 floor (10.9%) verifiable per state. (A2) Co-funded interconnection and transmission program targeting AZ and TX: the two states whose 2050 gaps (11.7 and 9.1 pp) are the largest and only ones at or near the 10-pp decision threshold; TX already has the largest wind base in the compact (195,455 B Btu, 2009) and AZ the fastest demand growth (2.8%/yr), so grid access is their binding constraint, not resource. (A3) Compact efficiency fund targeting TX and NM (intensities 10.59 and 9.70 kBtu/2000$ vs CA 4.61): a 1 pp/yr cut in demand drift raises 2050 renewable shares by ~0.5-1 pp in the high-d states, the cheapest share gain in the model, and directly supports NM's 2050 floor (gap 6.5 pp). (A4) Joint investment in storage, pumped hydro and geothermal (CA geothermal 127,461 B Btu; AZ hydro 62,731 B Btu, 2009) to lift the established base b_s, which is otherwise flat-to-falling (b_s in [-0.49, -0.00] pp/yr) - this is what turns rule A from a floor-decay line into a floor-growth line and is the only lever that helps CA 2050 (gap 5.5 pp). All four actions are consistent with the exchange-3 reading: they exist because the 2050 target for AZ (and near-for TX) is a genuine change-of-direction ask, while for CA/NM the same actions function as insurance that the floors hold.

tasks.task_description: Part III: One-page memo to the four governors summarizing findings and recommendations.
tasks.task_analysis: The memo must be one page, non-technical, decision-oriented: what the data says about where each state stands, what happens if nothing is done (the no-policy bands), what the targets are, and what the compact should actually do. It must use the exchange-3 reading (10 pp = the line between 'floor' and 'stretch') so each governor sees his state's verdict in plain terms, and it must not promise numbers outside the model's bands.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Memo content is a restatement, in plain language, of: I.C (California is the benchmark profile, 8.87% renewable in 2009); I.D (no-policy 2025/2050 bands per state); II.A (common targets 10.9% by 2025, 13.9% by 2050; per-state verdicts from the 10-pp rule: CA floors both years; AZ 2050 is the only true stretch, gap 11.7 pp; TX 2050 near-stretch, 9.1 pp; NM floors); II.B (the four actions and which state each one is for). No new numbers are introduced. Length is held to one printed page (~430 words).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: MEMO - To: Governors of California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas; From: Four-State Energy Compact; Re: Renewable energy targets 2025/2050. 1. Where we stand (2009 data, 50-year record): California runs the region's best renewable profile - 8.9% of total energy from renewables, the lowest per-capita use (217 million Btu/person), and the only state with a diversified base (hydro, geothermal, wood, plus growing wind and solar). Arizona sits at 6.9% but is losing ground as gas demand outgrows its hydro; New Mexico at 5.1%, almost all of it new wind on top of a small base; Texas at 3.1% - but Texas already holds the compact's largest wind fleet (more than the rest of the four states combined). 2. If we do nothing: our model (1990-2009 trends continued, new technologies at their capped recent pace) gives 2025 renewable shares of roughly 5-18% for California, 0.4-9% for Arizona, 3-12% for New Mexico, and 0.3-9% for Texas; by 2050 the drift lines are flat or falling for the mature sources, so every state's long-run share depends on how hard the wind/solar wave keeps growing. 3. The targets we propose: 10.9% of total energy from renewables by 2025 and 13.9% by 2050 - anchored on California's 2009 record plus a margin. By our 10-point decision rule (a gap under 10 points of renewable share is within forecast noise): for California, New Mexico, and Texas the 2025 target is a floor, not a stretch; for Arizona the 2050 target is the one real stretch (11.7 points above its drift) and Texas is a near-stretch (9.1 points). 4. What the compact will do: (a) a jointly administered renewable procurement standard so the 2025 floor is verifiable in each state; (b) a co-funded transmission and interconnection program aimed at Arizona and Texas, where the wind is already built but cannot reach the load; (c) an efficiency fund for Texas and New Mexico, the two states using twice as much energy per dollar of output as California - every point of demand growth we shave is a point of renewable share we do not have to build; (d) joint investment in storage, pumped hydro and geothermal to hold the mature base flat instead of letting it decay. In short: the 2025 target is credible for all four of us; the 2050 target is where this compact earns its keep - and it is achievable if Arizona and Texas get the grid money, and Texas and New Mexico get the efficiency money, by 2020.
